At the cooperative bank branch in the kasba, the pension-day queue stretched out to the tea stall. Lokesh, the branch manager, watched his new clerk, Siddharth, deal with old Tukaram kaka, who was shouting that his pension had been stolen.
Siddharth didn't shout back. He pulled up the passbook, found that the amount had gone into an old account, explained it slowly in Marathi, and walked kaka to the next counter to fix it.
Afterwards Lokesh said, "Good job." Siddharth shrugged. "Anyone could have done it. I still don't know half the software."
The words had bounced straight off. At closing time Lokesh tried again. "This morning, three things you did right. You didn't argue with kaka. You checked the old account before blaming anyone. And you walked him over yourself instead of pointing."
Siddharth looked at the floor, then up. "The old account... yes, I did think of that." He wrote something in the back of his register.

qa.q: Where had Tukaram kaka's pension gone?
qa.a: Into an old account.

qa.q: What did Lokesh feel when Siddharth shrugged off 'good job'?
qa.a: He felt concerned that vague praise had bounced off a doubting newcomer, and decided to be specific.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh's second attempt at praise land?
qa.a: It named three concrete actions Siddharth took, facts the doubting mind could not easily dismiss as kindness.

qa.q: What might Siddharth be feeling when he writes in the back of his register?
qa.a: He may feel quietly encouraged, holding on to concrete evidence that he handled the crisis well.

In Valentina's third week at the café in Porto, the espresso machine broke at 8 a.m. on a Saturday. Dalia, the manager, was stuck on the phone with the repair company and watched from the back.
Valentina didn't freeze. She put a sign on the counter, switched everyone to filter coffee and tea, handed free custard tarts to the grumpiest part of the queue, and kept the line moving with a joke about the machine needing a holiday.
When it was over she came to Dalia with red cheeks. "I'm sorry. I probably made a mess. I'm still so slow."
Dalia had told her "You're doing great" twice that week, and both times Valentina had only nodded. This time Dalia was specific. "You switched the menu within two minutes. You gave tarts to the people most likely to complain. Not one customer walked out. That was a manager's call."
Valentina blinked. "Not one?"
"I counted."

qa.q: What did Valentina switch everyone to?
qa.a: Filter coffee and tea.

qa.q: What was Dalia thinking when she chose to be specific this time?
qa.a: Dalia felt frustrated that 'you're doing great' had not reached Valentina, and hoped concrete facts would reassure her.

qa.q: What made Dalia's feedback something Valentina could accept?
qa.a: It listed exact actions and one fact, that not one customer walked out, which is harder to dismiss than general praise.

qa.q: What is Valentina feeling when she apologises with red cheeks?
qa.a: She feels anxious and embarrassed, sure she made a mess, even though she handled the crisis well.

grounding: A café manager notices a doubting new hire discount vague praise and gives specific, honest feedback on what she did well.

In the women's ward of the district hospital, Binita, the nurse in charge, had noticed that Zubin, the new nursing assistant, said "sorry" about twenty times a shift.
On Tuesday night an elderly patient in bed 12 became confused and tried to pull out her drip. Zubin got there first. He held her hand, spoke softly to her about her grandchildren, kept the drip in place and pressed the call bell without leaving her side. By the time Binita arrived, the patient was calm.
At handover he said, "Sorry, I should have noticed earlier."
Binita had already learned that "well done" slid off him like water. So she said, "You stayed with her instead of running for help. You kept the line safe. You called me without letting go. That's exactly the order I'd want."
Zubin looked at her as if checking she meant it. Then he nodded slowly and, for once, didn't say sorry.

qa.a: Bed 12.

qa.a: She was concerned that he apologised constantly, a sign of self-doubt that made plain 'well done' slide off him.

qa.q: Why is Binita's feedback at handover effective?
qa.a: She named the exact steps Zubin took and their order, giving his doubting mind facts he could accept.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel when he doesn't say sorry for once?

Elizabeth

"What answer?"
"About the vendor delay. You wrote 'check the customs date' on your pad. Then Neha said the same thing ten minutes later and the boss loved it."
"She said it better."

Vikas stirred his dal. "Everyone in that room sounds so sure. Neha, Prakash, even the intern. I sit there thinking, if I say something wrong, they'll all know I don't belong."

Four months into the agency, I've noticed something about myself I don't like. In every review, Avni talks first. She says things like, "I'm not sure, but what if the logo had more space?" and everyone leans in. I sit there with three ideas in my notebook and a voice in my head saying they're obvious, or wrong, or both.
I compare my inside, which is all doubt, with everyone else's outside, which looks like confidence. It isn't a fair match, but it doesn't feel unfair while it's happening.
Last week the creative director said, "Binita, you've been quiet," and I said, "I agree with Avni." I didn't, actually.
Now my name isn't on the new campaign. Of course it isn't. Nobody knows what I think. The silence is making me smaller, and the smaller I get, the more I believe I have nothing to add.

Supervisor's note, lab meeting, 9 October
Sudha has now sat through six lab meetings without speaking. Her bench work is careful; her notebook is the tidiest in the lab. But when we discuss results she looks down at her pad and lets Rekha answer, even about the assay Sudha ran herself.
Today I asked her directly about the odd reading in plate 3. She started, "It might be... no, it's probably nothing," and Rekha finished the thought. I spoke to Sudha afterwards. She said, "Everyone here talks like they've done a PhD already. I don't want to say something silly." She also said she assumed nobody noticed her work anyway.
My worry is the loop: the less she speaks, the less visible her work becomes, and the more she believes it isn't worth much.
Next step: I'll ask her to present plate 3 for five minutes next week, and go through it with her on Monday first.

She hesitated, then spoke for two minutes about waterlogging at the lower end. The room went quiet, then the senior officer nodded.
After the meeting Omkar walked with her to the jeep. "My first year here, I didn't say a word in these meetings for six months. I thought everyone knew more. Your salt report was the best catch of the season. Say that sort of thing out loud."

I'd been at the publishing house five weeks, nodding every time someone said "print run" or "proof pass", when the proofs of my first book came back with a note: Check the imprint page. I had no idea what an imprint page was.
I spent an hour searching old files, too scared to ask. Finally, ears burning, I walked to Tarun's desk. He's been in production for eight years. "This is probably a stupid question," I said, "but what exactly is the imprint page?"
He didn't laugh. He didn't sigh. He pulled a book off his shelf, flipped to the back of the title page and said, "This one. Copyright line, edition, printer. Takes five minutes. Want me to check yours after?"
That was it. No humiliation. I walked back feeling oddly light. Later I asked him two more things, and each time it felt less like confessing. I'm Amandeep, and I'm starting to think not knowing isn't a crime here.

qa.a: Keep asking small questions early, like the two later ones, rather than searching alone for an hour.

qa.q: How might Tarun have seen the question?
qa.a: Tarun likely saw it as an ordinary newcomer's question and was happy to help, without judging at all.

Something small but worth recording. Akash, three weeks in, has been silent in every stand-up and staying late most nights. Today, when Jaya mentioned the staging server, Akash half raised a hand and said, "Sorry, this is basic, but what's the difference between staging and production here?" His voice shook a little.
Jaya answered plainly: "Staging is where we test; production is what customers see. Good question, actually. The names confuse everyone at first." Then she drew a quick box diagram on the whiteboard, and two others took photos of it.
I watched Akash's shoulders drop. At lunch he asked Jaya two more questions, and he left at six-thirty today, the first time since he joined.
Action for me: add a glossary page to our onboarding notes and ask Akash to help write it, since he has just found some of the gaps.

Thursday, 11 p.m.
Did it. Finally asked.
For two weeks everyone on the news desk has been saying "check the slug", "change the slug", and I've been nodding like I knew. Tonight the chief sub said, "Saurabh, fix the slug on page four," and I froze at my screen.
So I leaned over to Chaitanya and whispered, "What's a slug? Sorry." My heart was going like a drum. I was sure Chaitanya would laugh, or tell the whole desk.
Chaitanya just said, "Oh, the short working name for the story, top left. Everyone asks that in week one," and went back to typing. That was all. Nobody looked up.
I fixed it in thirty seconds. I spent two weeks terrified of a thirty-second answer.
Tomorrow I'm going to ask what a "widow" means on the layout. I think.

passage:
Sunday, 21 July
Rashmi started on our team on Monday, and every time she said "sorry, dumb question," I heard myself from two years ago. I used to keep a list of words to look up secretly in the washroom.
On Wednesday I took her for chai and told her the washroom story. She laughed so hard she spilled some on her kurta. Then I showed her my old notebook with "what is a sprint??" written on the first page, both question marks and all.
Funny thing: while explaining the release process to her, I got one step wrong, and she caught it from the manual. Two years ago that would have wrecked my week. Today I said, "Nice catch, you're right," and we fixed it together.
I don't know everything. I'm fine with that now. And being the person someone asks feels like more proof that I belong here than any appraisal did.
Amandeep

qa.q: What was written on the first page of the old notebook?
qa.a: What is a sprint??

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel when Rashmi caught the mistake?
qa.a: Amandeep felt calm and even pleased, able to say 'nice catch' without the old panic.

qa.q: Why does helping Rashmi strengthen Amandeep's own sense of belonging?
qa.a: Being the one who explains and shares the old notebook shows Amandeep how far things have come, which feels like stronger proof than any appraisal.

qa.q: What is Rashmi's first week like after the chai?
qa.a: Rashmi feels relieved and more at ease, knowing a senior once felt just as lost 🙂

grounding: A young professional accepts not knowing everything and helps a newcomer, which confirms their own belonging.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
subtype: Stage 1: The news and the glow [Actor]
passage:
Tuesday. The director called Akash into the glass room and said the words he had waited four years for: "We'd like you to lead the payments team." He walked out trying to look calm and went straight to the stairwell to call his mother. She cried on the phone. So did he, a little.
Friday. His old college friend Saurabh booked a table at the Andhra place they used to go to as interns. The whole team came, clapping as he walked in. Someone had printed "Lead Engineer Akash" on a paper crown. He wore it all evening.
Sunday. At home, his father, who never said much, told the neighbours at the gate, "My son is managing people now." Akash overheard from the balcony and felt something warm settle in his chest. After all the late nights, it felt earned. Fair. His.

qa.q: What was printed on the paper crown?
qa.a: Lead Engineer Akash.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling when he overheard his father on Sunday?
qa.a: He felt proud and validated, a warm sense that the promotion was a fair reward for years of effort.

qa.q: What could Akash do in this glow to prepare well for the new role?
qa.a: Enjoy the moment, and also ask his old teammates what they need from a lead before the real work begins.

qa.q: What is the celebration like for Saurabh?
qa.a: Saurabh is happy and proud for an old friend, remembering their intern days at the same restaurant.

grounding: Over a week a well-liked engineer made team lead feels proud and validated as family and friends celebrate a reward earned.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
subtype: Stage 1: The news and the glow [Actor]
passage:
Rafiq, you look exactly like I did the day they made me shift supervisor at the textile mill in Coimbatore. I was twenty-five. Pallavi, the first woman supervisor on that floor in thirty years.
The manager read my name at the morning meeting, and the women from my old line started clapping before he finished. I had worked seven years on those looms. Seven years of double shifts. That evening my mother made payasam and sent some to every house on our street. My father, who had never once asked about my work, put on his good shirt and walked me to the bus the next morning.
I felt I had climbed a hill with my own hands. And I had. I let myself feel that fully.
But that same week I had to choose how I would treat the women I'd worked beside. That choice is the rest of the story, and you are about to face it too.

qa.q: How many years had Pallavi worked on the looms?
qa.a: Seven years.

qa.q: How did young Pallavi feel when her name was read out?
qa.a: She felt proud and validated, as if she had climbed a hill with her own hands after seven years.

qa.q: What choice in the story does Pallavi point to as the turning point?
qa.a: How she would treat the women she had worked beside, a choice that came in the same week as the promotion.

qa.q: What did the promotion mean to Pallavi's father in the story?
qa.a: He seemed quietly proud, putting on his good shirt and walking her to the bus, though he had never asked about her work.

grounding: An elder recalls being promoted to supervisor after years of hard work, feeling proud and validated as her family celebrated.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows

passage:
The email arrived while Himani was stuck at Itarsi junction, her train to Delhi seven hours late, phone at eleven per cent, the platform crowded with people asleep on bedrolls. Subject line: Promotion to Team Lead, Backend.
She read it three times. Four years of fixing other people's code at midnight, and someone had noticed. She wanted to shout, but the man on the bench beside her was asleep with his mouth open.
She had battery for exactly one call. Not her manager, not the team chat. She called Sonali.
"I'm a team lead," she whispered.
Sonali screamed so loudly that the sleeping man woke up. "I knew it! I told you they'd see it!"
Himani laughed and cried at the same time, and a chaiwala who had overheard handed her a free cup. "For the new boss," he said.
Her phone died two minutes later. She didn't mind at all.

qa.q: Where was Himani stuck when the email arrived?
qa.a: At Itarsi junction, her train to Delhi seven hours late.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling as she read the email three times?
qa.a: She felt proud and validated, thrilled that four years of midnight fixes had finally been noticed.

qa.q: What could Himani do once she is home to carry this glow wisely into the role?
qa.a: Celebrate with family, then thank the team she worked with and ask what they hope for from a new lead.

qa.q: What is the moment like for Sonali on the phone?
qa.a: Sonali is overjoyed and a little vindicated, having long believed Himani's work would be recognised.

grounding: Stuck on a delayed journey with a dying phone, a young engineer learns she is team lead and feels proud and validated as a friend celebrates.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
Three months after becoming lead, Farhan had developed a habit. Whenever the team debated anything in the Hyderabad office, he'd lean back and say, "Remember when I pushed for the cache layer last year? Everyone said no. I was right."
It had been a good call. It had also come up in six meetings this month.
He liked how the room went quiet when he started speaking now. He liked that Neelam, who used to argue with him over lunch, now said, "Whatever you think, Farhan." He didn't notice she said it with less energy each time.
On Friday Neelam presented a fix that cut load times by half. The director praised her in front of everyone. Farhan clapped, then sat through the rest of the meeting with a tight jaw. Nobody had mentioned that he approved the approach. He found himself waiting, all evening, for someone to say it.

qa.q: What decision does Farhan keep bringing up?
qa.a: When he pushed for the cache layer last year.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling when the director praised Neelam?
qa.a: He felt irritated and overlooked, expecting credit for approving the approach, which shows praise turning into an expectation.

qa.q: What could Farhan notice to catch this change in himself?
qa.a: That he mentioned the cache layer six times this month and waited all evening for credit; asking Neelam for her honest view would help.

qa.q: How does Neelam experience Farhan as a lead?
qa.a: Neelam has gone from arguing freely to saying 'whatever you think' with less energy, suggesting she feels less heard.

grounding: A new lead begins to see himself as the smart one, quotes his old decision, enjoys deference and starts to expect praise.

passage:
"Guess what the intern said today?" Imran asked, spooning biryani. "He said, 'Sir, how did you know the bug was in the queue?'"
"Sir?" Afreen raised an eyebrow. "Since when do they call you sir?"
"Since I became lead. I didn't ask them to. They just do." He smiled. "Honestly, I'm usually the smartest one in those rooms now."
"Usually?"
"Mostly. Remember the migration I planned last year? Still the best decision anyone's made on that team."
"You've told me about the migration four times this week."
"Because it's relevant!"
"And yesterday, when your director didn't comment on your slides, you sulked all evening."
"I did not sulk. I just expected... something. Some acknowledgement."
"You used to be happy when anyone said thank you. Now you're upset when they don't."
Imran put down his spoon. "That's not fair."
"Maybe. Think about it anyway."

qa.q: What did the intern call Imran?
qa.a: Sir.

qa.q: What does Imran's sulking over the director's silence show about how he feels?
qa.a: He feels hurt and entitled, since praise has shifted from a welcome surprise to something he expects.

qa.q: What could Imran do with Afreen's observation?
qa.a: Instead of defending himself, he could notice how often he quotes the migration and how he reacts when no one praises him.

qa.q: How does Afreen see the change in Imran?
qa.a: Afreen sees him becoming vain and harder to please, and cares enough to say so honestly, even at the risk of a quarrel.

grounding: A new lead at home boasts of being the smartest, quotes his old decision, enjoys being called sir and now expects praise.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
I can see it now, looking back at my first six months as creative lead, though at the time I'd have called it confidence. I began opening every review with "When I did the tea campaign..." as if everyone hadn't heard it. When juniors went quiet as I spoke, I read it as respect, and I liked it more than I'd admit.
The turning moment was small. Nirmala, who joined with me and used to tease me mercilessly, pitched an idea better than mine. The client loved it. And my first feeling wasn't pride in my team. It was a sour, childish thought: but I'm the lead.
That evening I understood I'd started expecting praise in every meeting, the way you expect the lights to come on when you press the switch. Missing it felt like an insult.
I'm Deepika. I'm not proud of that phase, but I'm glad I caught myself in it.

qa.q: How did Deepika open every review?
qa.a: With 'When I did the tea campaign...'

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when the client loved Nirmala's idea?
qa.a: Deepika felt a sour, childish jealousy, thinking 'but I'm the lead', instead of pride in the team.

qa.q: What could Deepika do now that the pattern is clear?
qa.a: Stop quoting the old campaign, credit Nirmala openly, and ask the juniors why they go quiet.

qa.q: How might Nirmala experience Deepika's change?
qa.a: Nirmala may feel distanced and less free to tease or challenge as before, even as Nirmala's ideas win.

grounding: A new creative lead looks back on seeing themself as the smart one, quoting past work, enjoying deference and expecting praise.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
It's been four months since I became lead, and I've stopped going to the Thursday lunch at the dhaba behind the office. I tell myself I'm busy, and I am. But I also didn't want to sit with Manjula and the others and hear them grumble about decisions I now make.
Last week Manjula asked me in the corridor why the deadline had moved. I said, "It's complicated, you don't need to worry about that level," and watched her face close. We used to share everything.
I've started keeping the planning notes to myself, too. Partly because I'm told to, and partly because it feels good to know things they don't.
Some distance comes with the job; I know that. But yesterday, walking past their table, I caught myself thinking they were small-minded. And I remembered that a year ago I sat at that table, grumbling the loudest. I'm Arohi, and I didn't like that thought.

qa.q: Which lunch has Arohi stopped going to?
qa.a: The Thursday lunch at the dhaba behind the office.

qa.q: What does Arohi feel when thinking the old friends are small-minded?
qa.a: Arohi feels a superior, distant pride, then an uneasy pang of recognition at having sat at that same table a year ago.

qa.q: What could Arohi do to keep healthy distance without looking down on old friends?
qa.a: Rejoin the lunch now and then, give Manjula an honest, simple answer about the deadline, and keep only truly private things private.

qa.q: How might Manjula have felt when told not to worry about 'that level'?
qa.a: Manjula probably felt hurt and talked down to by someone who used to share everything with her.

grounding: A new lead skips lunches with old friends, talks down to them and shares less, sliding from natural distance into feeling above them.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
Manager's note for Monday's one-to-one with Rukmini
Some observations from the month since Rukmini became shift lead at the call centre.
She no longer takes breaks with her old batch. Ayesha, who trained with her and was her closest friend on the floor, told me she has stopped being invited for evening chai. On Thursday I heard Rukmini tell Ayesha, in front of two new joiners, "Just follow the script, don't try to think," in a tone I haven't heard from her before. Ayesha went quiet and redid the call.
Rukmini has also stopped sharing the weekly targets with the team, passing on only the numbers she thinks they need.
Some distance is normal when someone moves up, and I told her so when she started. This looks like more than distance. On Monday I'll ask her how the role feels, tell her plainly what I saw, and suggest she restart the team huddle she used to love.

qa.q: What did Rukmini tell Ayesha in front of the new joiners?
qa.a: Just follow the script, don't try to think.

qa.q: What might Rukmini be feeling in her new role to act this way?
qa.a: She may feel superior and a little anxious to prove her authority, which comes out as coldness toward old friends.

qa.q: What does the manager plan, and why is it a good step?
qa.a: Asking how the role feels, naming exactly what was seen and suggesting she restart the huddle gives her a chance to correct course.

qa.q: How is Ayesha affected by Rukmini's change?
qa.a: Ayesha feels hurt and humiliated, left out of chai and spoken down to in front of new joiners by her closest friend.

grounding: A manager notes a new shift lead who stops taking breaks with old friends, talks down to them and shares less.

passage:
Friday, late
Rashmi messaged again: "Coming for lunch at the canteen? Everyone's asking where you disappeared to 🙂" I said I had a call. I didn't. I ate at my desk and read the quarterly deck instead. Lunch with them is just gossip now, and they don't get what I'm dealing with.
In the afternoon Rashmi asked why her leave was rejected. I explained it slowly, like to a child, and she said, "I know how leave works, Nandini." Fine. Touchy.
I didn't tell the team about the reorganisation rumour, even though I used to tell Rashmi everything first. They don't need to know. Knowing first is part of the job now, isn't it?
Still, when I walked past the canteen at two and heard them laughing, something twisted in my stomach. I told myself I've just outgrown it.

qa.q: What reason did Nandini give Rashmi for skipping lunch?
qa.a: I had a call.

qa.q: What does the twist in Nandini's stomach suggest?
qa.a: It suggests loneliness and a pang of guilt beneath the story of having outgrown old friends.

qa.q: What could Nandini try before the gap widens?
qa.a: Accept the next lunch invite, apologise to Rashmi for the tone about leave, and share news with the team where possible.

qa.q: How might Rashmi see Nandini's new behaviour?
qa.a: Rashmi likely feels hurt and pushed away, talked down to by someone who used to tell her everything first.

grounding: A new lead skips lunches, talks down to an old friend and keeps news back, telling themself they have simply outgrown the group.
